analysis.one_liner: Gives oil and gas producers new tax credits, softer environmental rules, lower royalties on federal land, and freedom to export crude oil.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced past its referral to the Senate Finance Committee and died there when the 104th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have given tax breaks to companies that pump oil and gas in the United States — a credit per barrel produced, bigger depletion deductions, and faster writeoffs of drilling and exploration costs. It also would have eased rules for the industry: lower royalties on oil taken from federal land, a shorter window for the government to collect unpaid royalties, a lower financial-responsibility bar for offshore drilling facilities, and repeal of the ban on exporting American crude oil. It added new procedural rights for private property owners facing endangered-species and wetlands decisions, and required agencies to prepare detailed risk assessments before issuing major health, safety, and environmental rules.
analysis.who_benefits: Domestic oil and gas producers, particularly those operating low-output marginal wells and new wells, gain new per-barrel tax credits, expanded percentage depletion deductions, faster writeoffs of exploration and drilling costs, and expanded enhanced-recovery credits [S3]. Companies drilling offshore gain lower financial-responsibility requirements [S3], and companies holding federal leases gain reduced royalties and a six-year shield against royalty collection actions [S3]. Crude producers gain the right to sell oil to foreign buyers [S3]. Property owners facing wetlands and endangered-species restrictions gain appeal rights and potential compensation [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Creates a tax credit of $3 per barrel of oil and 50 cents per thousand cubic feet of gas from new wells and low-producing marginal wells, phased out as prices rise [S3].
Removes the net-income limit on percentage depletion for oil and gas and expands depletion eligibility and rates for marginal production [S3].

Allows immediate expensing of geological and geophysical exploration costs, expands the enhanced oil recovery credit to secondary methods and the minimum tax, and offers an optional five-year writeoff of intangible drilling costs [S3].
Lets the Interior Secretary reduce royalties owed on federal oil and gas leases and bars the government from collecting unpaid royalties more than six years back unless fraud is proven [S3].
Repeals statutory limits on exporting domestically produced crude oil, freeing producers to sell to the highest bidder abroad [S3].

Adds procedural rights for property owners facing wetlands and endangered-species decisions, including administrative appeals and compensation when an agency decision cuts a property's value by a third or more [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers would cover the cost of the new tax credits and the forgone revenue from lower royalties and expensing provisions [S3]. The public would bear the cost of weaker safeguards: lower liability coverage for offshore spills, less government ability to recover unpaid royalties on public lands, and slower or costlier enforcement of wetlands and endangered-species protections where compensation mandates apply [S2][S3].

drawbacks.text: The bill weakens financial responsibility rules for offshore oil facilities, allowing liability coverage of $35 million (up to $150 million only at a President's discretion), which shifts the risk of an offshore spill away from industry and toward taxpayers and coastal communities [S3].

The compensation mandate requires agencies to pay owners when environmental decisions cut a property's value by a third or more, and makes agencies reimburse the Treasury if they lose follow-on court cases, which could drain enforcement budgets and discourage protective decisions [S3].

Repealing the export ban on domestic crude, the six-year royalty-collection deadline, and agency entry/data rules all reduce the government's ability to recover what the public is owed for resources taken from federal lands and waters [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefits flow mainly to oil and gas producers in the form of tax credits, depletion deductions, lower royalties, and lighter spill-liability and royalty-enforcement rules, while the costs land on taxpayers through forgone revenue and on the public through weaker environmental and landowner-protection enforcement. Some provisions — administrative appeals for property owners, an arguably more transparent risk-assessment process — have plausible public benefits, but the compensation mandate could drain agency budgets and chill enforcement. The bill was written for one industry and never advanced past referral.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which never took it up, so it expired when the 104th Congress ended in early January 1997.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on February 16, 1995 by Senator Nickles, with Senators Inhofe and Dole, and read twice before being referred to the Finance Committee the same day [S1][S5].
No further action appears in the record: no hearings, no markup, no vote, and no floor consideration [S5].
The bill's substance combined oil and gas tax breaks with deregulation, royalty relief, property-rights procedures, and repeal of the crude oil export ban [S2].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas producers benefit from the bill's death only in the sense that taxpayers and the Treasury were spared the cost of its new credits, royalty reductions, and weakened royalty enforcement; no one gained materially from a bill that went nowhere, but the public was spared its provisions.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had only three Republican sponsors and never reached a vote, so no record exists of how the parties as a whole stood on it.

industries.note: The bill's core purpose is to shift money and risk toward oil and gas producers: new tax credits, expanded depletion deductions, faster writeoffs, lower royalties on federal leases, a shorter window for the government to collect unpaid royalties, weaker offshore spill-liability rules, and the freedom to export crude. For the public, this means higher tax expenditures and less recovery of public-land revenue.

Risk-assessment requirements, entry-consent rules, compensation mandates, and administrative appeals would slow and complicate enforcement of the Clean Water Act and Endangered Species Act, raising the cost of protecting habitat and wetlands on behalf of the public.

Property owners gain procedural rights and potential compensation when environmental rules restrict land use, but the compensation is paid from public funds and the measure is framed around the oil and gas industry's regulatory burdens.
